{{Short description|Mathematical concept}}
In [[mathematics]], for a [[sequence]] of complex numbers ''a''<sub>1</sub>, ''a''<sub>2</sub>, ''a''<sub>3</sub>, ... the '''infinite product'''

:<math>
\prod_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n = a_1 a_2 a_3 \cdots
</math>

is defined to be the [[limit of a sequence|limit]] of the [[Multiplication#Capital pi notation|partial products]] ''a''<sub>1</sub>''a''<sub>2</sub>...''a''<sub>''n''</sub> as ''n'' increases without bound. The product is said to ''[[Limit of a sequence|converge]]'' when the limit exists and is not zero. Otherwise the product is said to ''diverge''.  A limit of zero is treated specially in order to obtain results analogous to those for [[Infinite series|infinite sums]]. Some sources allow convergence to 0 if there are only a finite number of zero factors and the product of the non-zero factors is non-zero, but for simplicity we will not allow that here. If the product converges, then the limit of the sequence ''a''<sub>''n''</sub> as ''n'' increases without bound must be 1, while the converse is in general not true.

The best known examples of infinite products are probably some of the formulae for [[pi|&pi;]], such as the following two products, respectively by [[Viète]] ([[Viète's formula]], the first published infinite product in mathematics) and [[John Wallis]] ([[Wallis product]]):

:<math>\frac{2}{\pi} = \frac{ \sqrt{2} }{ 2 } \cdot \frac{ \sqrt{2 + \sqrt{2}} }{ 2 } \cdot \frac{ \sqrt{2 + \sqrt{2 + \sqrt{2}}} }{ 2 } \cdot \; \cdots = \prod_{n=1}^{\infty} \cos \frac{\pi}{2^{n+1}}</math>
:<math>\frac{\pi}{2} = \left(\frac{2}{1} \cdot \frac{2}{3}\right) \cdot \left(\frac{4}{3} \cdot \frac{4}{5}\right) \cdot \left(\frac{6}{5} \cdot \frac{6}{7}\right) \cdot \left(\frac{8}{7} \cdot \frac{8}{9}\right) \cdot \; \cdots = \prod_{n=1}^{\infty} \left( \frac{ 4n^2 }{ 4n^2 - 1 } \right). </math>

== Convergence criteria ==
The product of positive real numbers
:<math>\prod_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n</math>
converges to a nonzero real number if and only if the sum
:<math>\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \log(a_n)</math>
converges. This allows the translation of convergence criteria for infinite sums into convergence criteria for infinite products. The same criterion applies to products of arbitrary complex numbers (including negative reals) if the logarithm is understood as a fixed [[Complex logarithm#Branches of the complex logarithm|branch of logarithm]] which satisfies <math>\ln(1) = 0</math>, with the provision that the infinite product diverges when infinitely many ''a<sub>n</sub>'' fall outside the domain of <math>\ln</math>, whereas finitely many such ''a<sub>n</sub>'' can be ignored in the sum.

If we define <math>a_n=1+p_n</math>, the bounds

:<math>1+\sum_{n=1}^{N} p_n \le \prod_{n=1}^{N} \left( 1 + p_n \right) \le \exp \left( \sum_{n=1}^{N}p_n \right)</math>

show that the infinite product of ''a''<sub>''n''</sub> converges if the infinite sum of the ''p''<sub>''n''</sub> converges. This relies on the [[Monotone convergence theorem]]. We can show the converse by observing that, if <math>p_n \to 0</math>, then

:<math>\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{\log(1+p_n)}{p_n} = \lim_{x\to 0} \frac{\log(1+x)}{x} = 1,</math>

and by the [[limit comparison test]] it follows that the two series

:<math>\sum_{n=1}^\infty \log(1+p_n) \quad \text{and} \quad \sum_{n=1}^\infty p_n,</math>

are equivalent meaning that either they both converge or they both diverge.

If the series <math display="inline">\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \log(a_n)</math> diverges to <math>-\infty</math>, then the sequence of partial products of the ''a''<sub>''n''</sub> converges to zero.  The infinite product is said to '''diverge to zero'''.<ref>{{cite book | title=Methods of Mathematical Physics | series=Cambridge Mathematical Library | first1=Harold | last1=Jeffreys | author1-link=Harold Jeffreys | first2=Bertha Swirles | last2=Jeffreys | author2-link=Bertha Swirles | edition=3rd revised | publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] | year= 1999 | isbn=1107393671 | page=52 }}</ref>

For the case where the <math>p_n</math> have arbitrary signs, the convergence of the sum <math display="inline">\sum_{n=1}^\infty p_n</math> does not guarantee the convergence of the product <math display="inline">\prod_{n=1}^\infty (1+p_n)</math>. For example, if <math>p_n = \frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{\sqrt{n}}</math>, then <math display="inline">\sum_{n=1}^\infty p_n</math> converges, but <math display="inline">\prod_{n=1}^\infty (1 + p_n)</math> diverges to zero. However, if <math display="inline">\sum_{n=1}^\infty |p_n|</math> is convergent, then the product <math display="inline">\prod_{n=1}^\infty (1+p_n)</math> converges ''absolutely''–that is, the factors may be rearranged in any order without altering either the convergence, or the limiting value, of the infinite product.<ref name="Trench1999">{{cite journal |last1=Trench |first1=William F. |date=1999 |title=Conditional Convergence of Infinite Products |url=http://ramanujan.math.trinity.edu/wtrench/research/papers/TRENCH_RP_93.PDF |journal=American Mathematical Monthly |volume=106 |issue=7 |pages=646–651 |doi= 10.1080/00029890.1999.12005098|access-date=December 10, 2018 }}</ref> Also, if <math display="inline">\sum_{n=1}^\infty |p_n|^2</math> is convergent, then the sum <math display="inline">\sum_{n=1}^\infty p_n </math> and the product <math display="inline">\prod_{n=1}^\infty (1+p_n)</math> are either both convergent, or both divergent.<ref name="Knopp">{{cite book |last=Knopp |first=Konrad |date=1954 |title=Theory and Application of Infinite Series |url=https://archive.org/details/theoryandapplica031692mbp/page/n5 |location=London |publisher=Blackie & Son Ltd. |author-link=Konrad Knopp}}</ref>

==Product representations of functions==
{{main|Weierstrass factorization theorem}}

One important result concerning infinite products is that every [[entire function]] ''f''(''z'') (that is, every function that is [[holomorphic function|holomorphic]] over the entire [[complex number|complex plane]]) can be factored into an infinite product of entire functions, each with at most a single root.  In general, if ''f'' has a root of order ''m'' at the origin and has other complex roots at ''u''<sub>1</sub>, ''u''<sub>2</sub>, ''u''<sub>3</sub>, ... (listed with multiplicities equal to their orders), then

:<math>f(z) = z^m e^{\phi(z)} \prod_{n=1}^{\infty} \left(1 - \frac{z}{u_n} \right) \exp \left\lbrace \frac{z}{u_n} + \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{z}{u_n}\right)^2 + \cdots + \frac{1}{\lambda_n} \left(\frac{z}{u_n}\right)^{\lambda_n} \right\rbrace </math>

where ''λ''<sub>''n''</sub> are non-negative integers that can be chosen to make the product converge, and <math>\phi (z)</math> is some entire function (which means the term before the product will have no roots in the complex plane).  The above factorization is not unique, since it depends on the choice of values for ''λ''<sub>''n''</sub>.  However, for most functions, there will be some minimum non-negative integer ''p'' such that ''λ''<sub>''n''</sub> = ''p'' gives a convergent product, called the [[Weierstrass factorization theorem|canonical product representation]]. This ''p'' is called the ''rank'' of the canonical product. <!-- The ''genus'' is the (is it max? or min?) of the degree of φ and ''p''. --> In the event that ''p'' = 0, this takes the form

:<math>f(z) = z^m e^{\phi(z)} \prod_{n=1}^{\infty} \left(1 - \frac{z}{u_n}\right).</math>

This can be regarded as a generalization of the [[fundamental theorem of algebra]], since for polynomials, the product becomes finite and <math>\phi (z)</math> is constant.

In addition to these examples, the following representations are of special note:

{| class="wikitable"
! Function
! Infinite product representation(s)
! Notes
|-
| Simple pole
| <math>\begin{align}
    \frac{1}{1 - z} &= \prod_{n=1}^\infty e^{z^n/n} \\
 &= \prod_{n=0}^\infty \left(1+z^{2^n}\right)
  \end{align}</math>
|
|-
| [[Sinc function]]
| <math>\frac{\sin \pi z}{\pi z} =\prod_{n=1}^{\infty} \left(1 - \frac{z^2}{n^2}\right)</math>
| This is due to [[Euler]]. [[Wallis product|Wallis' formula for π]] is a special case of this.
|-
| [[Reciprocal gamma function]]
| <math>\begin{align}
    \frac{1}{\Gamma(z)} &= z e^{\gamma z} \prod_{n=1}^{\infty} \left(1 + \frac{z}{n}\right) e^{-\frac{z}{n}} \\
    &= z \prod_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1+\frac{z}{n}}{\left(1+\frac{1}{n}\right)^z}
  \end{align}</math>
| [[Schlömilch]]{{clarify|date=September 2022}}
|-
| [[Weierstrass sigma function]]
| <math>\sigma(z) = z\prod_{\omega \in \Lambda_{*}} \left(1-\frac{z}{\omega}\right)e^{\frac{z^2}{2\omega^2}+\frac{z}{\omega}}</math>
| Here <math>\Lambda_{*}</math> is the lattice without the origin.
|-
| [[Q-Pochhammer symbol]]
| <math>(z;q)_\infty = \prod_{n=0}^\infty (1-zq^n)</math>
| Widely used in [[q-analog]] theory. The [[Euler function]] is a special case.
|-
| [[Ramanujan theta function]]
| <math>\begin{align}
    f(a,b) &=\sum_{n=-\infty}^\infty a^{\frac{n(n+1)}{2}} b^{\frac{n(n-1)}{2}} \\
    &= \prod_{n=0}^\infty (1+a^{n+1}b^n)(1+a^nb^{n+1})(1-a^{n+1}b^{n+1})
  \end{align}</math>
| An expression of the [[Jacobi triple product]], also used in the expression of the Jacobi [[theta function]]
|-
| [[Riemann zeta function]]
| <math>\zeta(z) = \prod_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{1 - p_n^{-z}}</math>
| Here ''p''<sub>''n''</sub> denotes the ''n''th [[prime number]]. This is a special case of the [[Euler product]].
|}

The last of these is not a product representation of the same sort discussed above, as ''ζ'' is not entire. Rather, the above product representation of ''ζ''(''z'') converges precisely for Re(''z'') &gt; 1, where it is an analytic function. By techniques of [[analytic continuation]], this function can be extended uniquely to an analytic function (still denoted ''ζ''(''z'')) on the whole complex plane except at the point ''z'' = 1, where it has a simple [[pole (complex analysis)|pole]].
